title: TB8-06398
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): The appellants XXXX XXXX (the principal appellant "PA"), his spouse, XXXX XXXX (the female appellant "FA") and their minor son, XXXX XXXX (the minor appellant "MA"), citizens of Azerbaijan, appeal a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying their claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: The appellants XXXX XXXX (the principal appellant "PA"), his spouse, XXXX XXXX (the female appellant "FA") and their minor son, XXXX XXXX (the minor appellant "MA"), citizens of Azerbaijan, appeal a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying their claim for refugee protection. They ask the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) to either grant their claim for protection or refer the matter back to the RPD for redetermination. They have not provided new evidence. They have not requested an oral hearing.

Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (the "Act")i, the RAD confirms the decision of the RPD that the PA and FA are excluded from protection pursuant to section 98 of the Act, as it incorporates Article 1E of the United Nations Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees (the "Refugee Convention").ii The RAD further confirms the decision of the RPD that the appellants are not Convention refugees pursuant to section 96 of the Act, nor are they persons in need of protection pursuant to section 97 of the Act.
In XXXX 2017, the appellants applied for and acquired visas to the United States (USA).

In XXXX 2017, the appellants applied for and acquired tourist visas to Canada. In their application, they described, [v]isiting Canada have been and still is my dream having already travelled throughout vast majority of Europe as well as US and also working for a worldwide corporations I get to meet new and exciting people from all over the world. All of them were amazed by the beauty of Canada, by the sightseeing, countless lakes, greenest parks, friendly people who will take their time to suggest where one must go to get the best experience and memories from Vancouver.iii
In XXXX 2017, the appellants travelled to the USA. They did not seek asylum there. In this regard, the PA advised Canadian border officials, "I do not want my son to grow up in the United States".iv

In XXXX 2017, the appellants travelled to Toronto, Canada. They initiated a claim for refugee protection alleging a fear of persecution based upon their perceived political opinion. In particular, they allege the PA was "illegally detained" by local police in Azerbaijan and "beaten up pretty much everyday" between XXXX XXXX, 2017 to XXXX XXXX, 2017, inclusive.v

The appellants' claim before the RPD was heard over two days on November 15, 2017 and January 5, 2018. In a decision on February 8, 2018, the appellants' claim was rejected. The determinative issues were credibility, internal flight alternative (IFA), and exclusion pursuant to Article 1E of the Refugee Convention due to the PA and FA's permanent resident status in Kazakhstan.

The appellants argue the findings of the RPD were not reasonable or correct: (i) with respect to exclusion and risk in Kazakhstan, (ii) with respect to risk in Azerbaijan, and (iii) included breach of procedural fairness. The RAD is not persuaded the RPD erred. The RPD correctly concluded the appellants failed to credibly establish their claim for protection against Azerbaijan. The RPD also correctly determined the PA and FA were excluded from refugee protection. ANALYSIS Role of the RAD
The RAD is to review raised issues with the RPD's findings of law, fact (and mixed fact and law), which raised no issue of credibility of oral evidence, applying the correctness standard.vi

In assessing the credibility of oral evidence, the RPD may have a meaningful advantage, as the RPD directly sees, observes, and selects questions to ask of the witnesses, etc. The Court has specifically reiterated that "significant deference is due to the findings of a tribunal"vii recognizing that "the role of this Court is a very limited one because the tribunal had the advantage of hearing the witnesses testify, observed their demeanor and is alive to all the factual nuances and contradictions in the evidence".viii
Finally, the panel notes an appeal to the RAD is not a de novo hearing, as the appellants have argued many of the same submissions already made to the RPD. Onus is on the Appellants

The onus is on the appellants to provide full and detailed submissions regarding the errors they allege the RPD made. Rule 3(3)(g) of the Refugee Appeal Division Rulesix specifically requires that an Appellant's Record must include "a memorandum that includes full and detailed submissions regarding: (i) the errors that are the grounds of the appeal, (ii) where the errors are located in the written reasons for the ... [RPD's] decision that the appellant is appealing or in the transcript or in any audio or other electronic recording of the ... [RPD's] hearing...."

The appellants have failed to do so. Instead, the appellants have attacked the RPD's decision by resubmitting their representations already made to the RPD. The role of the RAD is not to provide the appellants a "second chance" to present their claim.
The RAD has nevertheless independently reviewed the evidence and addressed the appellants' main arguments, as follows. The RPD Findings Exclusion - Kazakhstan

The RPD determined the PA and FA were excluded from refugee protection pursuant to Article 1E of the Refugee Convention. In particular, the RPD concluded: [i]n the present case the adult claimants continue to have valid permanent resident cards for a third country, namely Kazakhstan, at the time of the hearing. In reaching my decision that the adult claimants are excluded under Section 1E of the Convention, I considered the factors as set out in the Shamlou and Zeng cases, and I have given probative weight to the Minister's disclosure which included correspondence from the Kazakh Consulate in Canada. Therefore, based on the foregoing analysis I find that the adult claimants are excluded under Article 1E of the Convention.x

The appellants argue the RPD erred because the PA and FA have lost their status in Kazakhstan because they have been out of the country for more than three years. They also argue the RPD failed to question them about this issue and thus to know the case against them.
The RAD notes the appellants made the same submissions about their lost status before the RPD. The appellants have failed to demonstrate how the RPD erred in its analysis or findings.

Having reviewed the evidence, there is nothing before the RAD that suggests the RPD failed to correctly consider the evidence (including the appellants' testimony and their country documents, such as the print out of a Kazakh website) in accordance with the leading jurisprudence. In this regard, the RPD demonstrated a detailed and thorough review of the evidence, including an assessment of the appellants' testimony and their claim that their status had expired.

The RAD further notes the appellants' hearing extended to two dates and almost four hours of testimony. The RPD and the appellants' counsel asked many detailed questions of the adult appellants, including about their current status in Kazakhstan and any fear they may have in returning there. Moreover, the Minister of Immigration, Refugee and Citizenship Canada intervened on the exclusion basis.xi As such, the RAD does not find persuasive the appellants' argument that the RPD erred by failing to give them an opportunity to know the case against them.

Further, the RPD specifically noted, that the issue of credibility is pivotal in the determination of this case, particularly with respect to how the PC was able to obtain his permanent resident status and through him the SC claimant's permanent resident status, and whether their permanent resident status is currently valid.xii[emphasis added]

The RAD further notes - only upon the RPD panel's request - the appellants submitted their Kazakhstan permanent resident (PR) permits,xiii which clearly indicated the PA's status is valid until XXXX XXXX XXXX/2020 and the FA's status is valid until XXXX XXXX XXXX/2022. The RPD noted, "[o]n the face of neither of these cards examined at the hearing, is any indication that because the PC no longer works in Kazakhstan or has not been in Kazakhstan since some time in 2014 that he has lost his permanent resident status".xiv The appellants have not challenged this specific finding.

As also noted by the RPD, the Minister's materials indicate PR holders have the right to return to Kazakhstan as long as the PR ID card is valid. The PA and FA hold valid PR ID cards, which have not been revoked. As further noted by the RPD, the PA and FA's PR cards do not need to be renewed, since they are still valid until 2020 and 2022. In this regard, the appellants have failed to provide any evidence that they have lost their status. For example, the appellants have not demonstrated that they have taken any steps to confirm their current status and any potential renewal concerns with any government officials or legal authorities etc. Further, their allegation that they will be unable to return to Kazakhstan is unsubstantiated. In this regard, the RAD notes the PA testified that Azari citizens do not need a visa to enter Kazakhstan. He also confirmed that he could travel freely in Kazakhstan and enter and exit the country without any problems. He also previously lived and worked in Kazakhstan with no apparent problems. The RAD accordingly sees no reason to interfere with the RPD's finding that the appellants failed to establish that they no longer have PR status in Kazakhstan.

The RPD also determined that permanent residents of Kazakhstan enjoy similar rights to Kazakh nations, including the rights to free movement and travel, work pension and social security payments. The appellants have not challenged this finding. The RAD sees no reason to interfere with this uncontested finding.

The RPD also asked the adult appellants several questions about any risk of return to Kazakhstan. The RPD noted: [t]he claimants both testified that they did not "like" living in Kazakhstan. The SC testified that there were no "trees" and the people were not nice in Kazakhstan. The PC testified that when he would enter pubs and restaurants, people stared at him and that although Kazakhstan is a good place to make money, he would not consider it as a place to settle down with his son and his wife. The test for seeking for protection is not green space or whether the claimants enjoy living in a third country where they have a right of residency.xv

The RPD concluded the appellants failed to provide any evidence they would face any risk of harm in Kazakhstan or, that if they became victims of common crime, there would be no state protection available to them. The appellants have not challenged this finding. The RAD sees no reason to interfere with this uncontested finding, as the RAD also agrees with it.

Having independently reviewed the evidence, including the testimony and the documentary evidence, the RAD finds no error in the RPD's analysis and exclusion determination regarding the PA and FA. This is a determinative issue in their claim. Inclusion - Azerbaijan

The RPD also assessed the merits of the appellants' claim against Azerbaijan. The RPD determined the appellants had not met their burden to establish their claim for protection. The RPD had a number of credibility concerns with the appellants and their allegations of persecution, including the PA's alleged perceived political profile and the lack of corroborating documents.

The appellants vaguely argue the RPD erred by failing to accurately assess the totality of evidence with detailed reasons. They also argue the PA's testimony "fell within those recognized as reasonable by jurisprudence".xvi

The RAD (again) notes the onus is on the appellants to provide full and complete submissions on how the RPD erred. The appellants have failed to do so. Instead, the appellants have provided submissions on alternative interpretations of the evidence i.e., that the PA's testimony was reasonable. They are thus essentially asking the RAD to reweigh the evidence in their favour. This is not the role of the RAD.

Having nevertheless independently reviewed the evidence, the RAD does not agree with the appellants' argument. There is no evidence the RPD failed to consider the appellants' evidence and their particular circumstances in considering their claim. Indeed, the RPD also afforded the appellants additional time for their hearing, as their hearing took place over two sittings and almost four hours of testimony. The RPD reasons for decision are similarly very thorough, directly related to the testimony and other evidence, and intelligible.

Further, the RPD had a number of credibility concerns with the appellants and their allegations of persecution, which the appellants have not contested. For example, the RPD concluded the PA was not a credible witness and embellished his testimony. The RPD also drew a negative credibility inference from the omission of the allegation the PA was on a "black list" in Azerbaijan. The appellants have not challenged these findings. The RAD sees no reason to interfere with these uncontested findings, as the RAD also agrees with them.

The RAD also specifically notes with regards to the allegations and timeline of evidence: * On XXXX XXXX, 2017, the PA's cousin "XXXX" was allegedly imprisoned about not paying taxes. XXXX was the owner/employer of the PA's workplace; * The PA allegedly wrote a letter of complaint to the Presidential Administration about his cousin's treatment; * On XXXX XXXX, 2017, the PA allegedly received a notice in the mail to appear at the Prosecutor's Office on XXXX XXXX, 2017; * On XXXX XXXX, 2017, the PA was allegedly questioned, beaten, and detained by authorities; * On XXXX XXXX, 2017, the MA was issued a passport; * On XXXX XXXX, 2017 until XXXX XXXX, 2017, the PA was allegedly detained and beaten; * Upon the PA's release from detention (at the end of May 2017), he decided to flee the country; * In XXXX 2017, the appellants applied for and obtained visas to the USA; * In XXXX 2017, the appellants applied for and obtained visas to Canada; and, * In XXXX 2017, the appellants left the country for the USA and then Canada.

As noted by the RPD, the appellants failed to provide any corroborating evidence from XXXX, who is allegedly the main reason for the appellants' allegations of persecution. When asked about his lack of evidence from his cousin, the PA simply responded he did not want to get evidence from him. The RPD further noted the appellants also failed to provide a copy of the letter of complaint the PA allegedly wrote and delivered to the President's Administration about XXXX detention. He testified he did not have a copy. The RPD drew a negative credibility inference due to the lack of corroborating evidence. The RAD agrees and does not find the PA's response about the lack of these documents to be reasonable nor credible under the circumstances. As such, the RAD finds the appellants' failure to provide any corroborating evidence from XXXX and/or a copy of the PA's purported letter of complaint about XXXX detention, and the lack of any efforts to obtain such documents, added to the RAD's own concerns with the credibility of the appellants and their allegations of persecution.

Accordingly, based upon its own review of the evidence in its entirety, the RAD does not find on a balance of probabilities, that the appellants provided sufficient credible and trustworthy evidence to establish their allegations of persecution due to the PA's perceived political profile. The appellants did not credibly establish that the PA is known and/or wanted by the authorities or any state agents for political reasons or otherwise. In this regard, the RAD also notes XXXX has apparently left the country and his business is run by new owners. Indeed, the PA worked for the new owners with no apparent problems up until his departure from the country. The appellants also had no problems leaving the country in September 2017 despite the PA allegedly being on a "blacklist".
The RPD found the appellant and his allegations to be generally lacking in credibility; having independently reviewed the evidence, the RAD has reached the same conclusion.

The RAD accordingly finds that there is not a serious possibility the appellants would be persecuted if returned to Azerbaijan pursuant to section 96 of the Act. The panel similarly finds that, on a balance of probabilities, the appellants would not be personally subjected to a danger of torture, or face a risk to life, or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in Azerbaijan pursuant to section 97 of the Act. Internal Flight Alternative

In the alternative, the RPD also determined the appellants had a viable IFA available to them in their country, specifically in Ganja, which is the second largest city in Azerbaijan. This is a determinative issue in the appellants' claim.
The appellants vaguely argue the RPD erred because the PA is "of ongoing concern to agents of the state", which generally negates an IFA.xvii

Having independently reviewed the evidence, the RAD does not agree with the appellants' argument. In coming to this conclusion, the RAD is guided by the jurisprudence and the particular circumstances of this claim.

The question of whether an IFA exists is an integral part of the Convention refugee definition. It arises when a refugee claimant who otherwise meets all the elements of the Convention refugee definition in his or her home area of the country nevertheless is not a Convention refugee because the person has an IFA elsewhere in that country.xviii

The jurisprudence has clearly established if there is a safe haven for refugee claimants in their own country, where they could live free from harm, they are expected to avail themselves of it, unless they can show it is objectively unreasonable or unduly harsh for them to do so.

The RAD finds the appellants failed to establish with sufficient trustworthy and credible evidence that the new business owners nor any state agents have any interest, motivation, means or resources to pursue them in Ganja. The RAD accordingly finds no error in the RPD's conclusion that the appellants had not met their burden to establish that there is a serious possibility of persecution for them in Ganja. The panel therefore finds that, on a balance of probabilities, the risk of the appellants being attacked or harmed in Ganja is not more than a mere possibility.

The RAD also agrees with the RPD that the appellants failed to meet the threshold of establishing it would be objectively unreasonable or unduly harsh for them to relocate to Ganja. In this regard, the panel is guided by the jurisprudence, such as in Thirunaukkarasu,xix which found that it is not enough for refugee claimants to say that they do not like the weather there or that they have no friends or relatives there or that they may not be able to find suitable work there. In this regard, the RAD notes the PA and FA are well-educated professionals and very well-travelled. They have travelled, resided, and worked in various international countries. They are fluent in many languages, including English. They also have family in Azerbaijan.

As stated by the Court of Appeal, "[t]here will always be hardship with relocation, but the threshold for unreasonable is very high and requires conditions that would jeopardize the life and safety of a claimant."xx The courts have repeatedly outlined that 'objectively unreasonable' is a very high threshold and requires, at a minimum, the proof of adverse conditions which would jeopardize the life and safety of the appellants in relocating, demonstrated based on actual and concrete evidence.xxi The appellants have not provided any such evidence. Accordingly, upon its own independent review of the evidence, the RAD finds the appellants have not met their onus of establishing this very high threshold. The RAD further notes the "burden does not fall on the RAD to explain why the proposed IFA would be safe" for the appellants.xxii The onus is on the appellants to demonstrate why the proposed IFA is not reasonable. The appellants have not demonstrated the high threshold to do so.

Finally, as held in Calderon v. Canadaxxiii the finding that there is a viable IFA is determinative of a refugee claim: [t]he question of the existence of an IFA is determinative of the matter. As set out in Irshad, above, at paragraph 21, the concept of an IFA is an inherent part of the Convention refugee definition. In order to be considered a Convention refugee, an individual must be a refugee from a country, not from a region of a country. Therefore, where an IFA is found, a claimant is not a refuge[e] or a person in need of protection....

The panel therefore finds that there is not a serious possibility that the appellants would be persecuted if they returned to Azerbaijan pursuant to section 96 of the Act. The panel similarly finds that, on a balance of probabilities, the appellants would not be personally subjected to a danger of torture or face a risk to life or risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in Azerbaijan pursuant to section 97 of the Act.
On the basis of the findings noted above and after its own assessment of all the evidence in the record, the RAD finds that the RPD's exclusion and inclusion determinations are correct.

Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the Act, the RAD confirms the decision of the RPD that the appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection. The RAD also confirms the decision of the RPD that the PA and FA are excluded from refugee protection pursuant to section 98 of the Act, as it incorporates Article 1E of the Refugee Convention.

The appeal is dismissed. (signed) "D. Goff" D.
